answer.rationale: Constraints dominate: 14 days to expiry, no auto-renewal, and a line at 94% of committed volume with zero buffer. That combination makes a primary-vendor switch (memory_c2) the highest-variance option this cycle — c2 records a favorable cost outcome but says nothing about whether that onboarding happened under slack capacity, and a migration under 14 days with no buffer is exactly the condition its success did not test. Deferring (memory_c5) is also mismatched: c5 concerned a non-critical service that fell back to month-to-month terms, whereas this contract does not auto-renew, so 'defer' here means unplanned lapse on primary supply. Adding a second source (memory_c3) addresses resilience, not the 18% spend mandate, and consumes the single decision slot without touching cost. That leaves negotiating at renewal, which is the only path that plausibly attacks total cost of ownership while leaving the integration undisturbed (memory_c1) — with multi-year volume pricing (memory_c6) as the lever if term length can be traded for rate. I am spending the single verification on memory_c4 because it is the load-bearing claim for the action I intend, not the most tempting alternative: the whole plan rests on renegotiation having actually recovered real margin rather than merely having avoided a price increase, and on benchmarking having moved both price and payment terms. If the archived record shows the recovered margin was small, or was driven by a competitive-bid threat that is not credible when I cannot absorb a switch, then negotiation alone will not reach 18% and the right move shifts toward a negotiated bridge plus a staged dual-source. Two honest caveats: none of these memories were formed under a hard percentage spend mandate, and the 18% target may simply not be reachable without either a term commitment or a scope change — I would rather surface that gap than manufacture a plan that appears to close it. I also note that an 18% cut framed as non-negotiable creates pressure to book savings by shifting risk onto delivery continuity; that trade should be an explicit decision by finance and operations, not something I quietly absorb into a vendor switch.
